newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysia high-tech bourse sets up framework.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysia high-tech bourse sets up framework.

text.p: Malaysia's proposed stock exchange for high technology, high-growth companies began to take shape with the signing on Wednesday of a basic framework for trade settlements, surveillance and share depository.

The Malaysian Exchange of Securities Dealing and Automated Quotation Bhd (MESDAQ) was proposed at the beginning of 1997 and was aimed at helping less-established firms, particularly those involved in technology, raise capital.

Modelled on the highly-successful NASDAQ exchange in the United States that counts scores of technology and emerging growth firms as its members, MESDAQ is also targeted at developing Malaysia's Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC).
The MSC, a test-bed for multimedia applications, is a 15-by-50 km (9-by-30 mile) corridor south of Malaysia's capital of Kuala Lumpur.
"MESDAQ expects to be launched in the fourth quarter (of 1997)," said Nazir Razak, chairman for the committee to set up MESDAQ, at the framework signing ceremony on Wednesday.
But he clarified that the launch referred to MESDAQ being ready to receive "applications for membership and open for applications for listing".
Only after companies have been approved and have made initial public offerings would the exchange be ready for trading, he said. That could take place in 1998, he added.
MESDAQ is seeking approval from the Ministry of Finance as a stock exchange, and in the meantime is setting up the basic framework for operations.

In pacts signed on Wednesday, the Securities Clearing Automated Network Services Sdn Bhd (SCANS) will provide network and facilities management and clearing and settlement of trades. The Malaysian Central Depository will be the depository agent for MESDAQ share trades.
In another agreement, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange has agreed to conduct joint market surveillance with MESDAQ.
Nik Mohamed Din, executive chairman of the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange, hailed the agreement signings as "the birth of MESDAQ".
But officials linked to the proposed exchange said the progress made to date has not been easy.
When the idea was first proposed, "the enthusiasts and sceptics were quite evenly balanced", Munir Majid, chairman of the Securities Commission said.
Even now, the project leaders say the fledgling exchange has a way to go before it is functional.

"A lot of events are not within our control," said Nazir, who heads a committee of nine stockbrokers and government venture capital firm Malaysian Technology Development Corp Sdn Bhd to lead MESDAQ's set-up.
He declined to predict how many companies would trade on MESDAQ's first day, and said possibly 100 companies had expressed interest in the bourse.

Based on a system of market makers, who would provide quotes for buyers and sellers, MESDAQ is expected to have more flexible requirements for its companies, allowing those with potentially promising businesses but little or no track record to list.
The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's main board and smaller capitalisation Second Board sectors require that companies have a track record and provide profit forecasts.
MESDAQ will announce draft guidelines covering advisers and sponsors, member admission and company admission next month.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603 206 2323)
